Make VnExpress a preferred source to prioritise our updates in your Google search results Vietnam can turn global supply chain diversification into long-term economic gains by moving into advanced manufacturing, technology and innovation, says Ernesto Torres Cantú, Citi's Head of International. Ernesto Torres Cantú oversees Citi's businesses outside North America, giving him a broad perspective on global trade, investment and financial markets.
In October, he attended the World Bank Group and International Monetary Fund Annual Meetings in Thailand before visiting Vietnam. In this interview, he discusses Vietnam's position in shifting global supply chains, opportunities to attract higher-value investment, the overseas expansion of Vietnamese companies and AI's impact on banking.
How is Vietnam positioned amid changes in global trade and supply chains?
Global trade is not declining; trade and production are shifting geographically.
Businesses are looking beyond costs and prioritizing resilience, speed and flexibility. The Covid-19 pandemic, geopolitical tensions and supply chain disruptions have accelerated efforts to diversify production locations, suppliers and markets.
Vietnam is well positioned to benefit. It sits at the heart of Asia's manufacturing ecosystem, has access to global markets through an extensive network of trade agreements and has a domestic market of more than 100 million people.
The country also benefits from its strategic location, economic management, ambitious reforms, fiscal discipline and sustained growth. A young, increasingly skilled workforce and rising education levels further strengthen its appeal to investors.
Vietnam has established a strong manufacturing base. The next step is to move up the value chain through advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, technology and innovation, while strengthening domestic industries and supply chains.
This aligns with the government's goals of improving productivity, accelerating digital transformation and attracting higher-value investment. Citi can help connect Vietnam with the capital, expertise and international markets needed to support these priorities.
Ernesto Torres Cantú, Citi's Head of International. Photo courtesy of him
Vietnam attracted US$50.4 billion in registered foreign direct investment in the first nine months of 2026, up 76% year on year. What is driving this momentum, and how can the country turn it into sustainable growth?
The figures reflect strong confidence in Vietnam, but investment volume is only part of the story. The more important question is how investment contributes to productivity, innovation and long-term development.
The next wave of foreign investment could extend beyond traditional export manufacturing into advanced electronics, semiconductors, digital infrastructure, data centers, renewable energy, logistics, healthcare and consumer industries.
Vietnam's reclassification to secondary emerging-market status should also help deepen its capital markets and broaden access to international investment.
Cost competitiveness has been important, but it will not be enough to attract the next generation of investment. Investors will increasingly look for reliable energy supplies, modern infrastructure, skilled workers, predictable regulations and strong domestic suppliers.
Vietnam has demonstrated its ability to attract international capital at scale. The opportunity now is to direct more investment into sectors that will shape its next stage of development, particularly advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, digital infrastructure, the energy transition and innovation.
During my visit, I met Deputy Prime Minister Nguyen Van Thang, State Bank of Vietnam Deputy Governor Nguyen Ngoc Canh and Deputy Minister of Finance Tran Quoc Phuong. We discussed how Citi could connect public-sector development priorities with international investment through our global network.
We also offer expertise in debt strategy, capital markets, investor engagement, hedging and project financing to help governments and institutions mobilize development funding while managing financial risks.
Vietnamese companies are increasingly expanding overseas. What will it take for more of them to become successful regional and global players?
As Vietnam's economy develops, more local companies are likely to become regional and global leaders. Success requires more than entering new markets: companies must coordinate capital, operations and risk management across countries.
Citi works with leading Vietnamese businesses on the financial and operational complexities of cross-border growth. For example, we supported Viettel's expansion in Peru through a $200 million financing facility with a six-year tenor. The financing helped Viettel Peru invest in infrastructure, pursue its long-term objectives and strengthen its position in the market.
Citi operates in more than 90 markets, combining local expertise with international connectivity. Our ambition is to be the leading bank for clients with cross-border needs, but trust must be earned every day.
How will AI and real-time payments reshape international banking and trade finance for businesses in Vietnam?
We are integrating AI across our businesses, with safety, compliance and responsible innovation as priorities. Our internal AI tools are used by nearly 180,000 employees across 87 countries and jurisdictions, and adoption is expected to grow.
Our service operations teams, for example, use CitiService Agent Assist to respond to client inquiries more quickly and accurately. AI has also been integrated into wholesale credit underwriting in 41 countries, enabling processing volumes four times higher than before.
Payments are evolving similarly. Clients increasingly expect cross-border transactions to be fast, transparent, trackable and available around the clock. For an internationally connected economy like Vietnam, these capabilities are particularly important as trade and investment flows expand.
Through Citi's network, clients in Vietnam can send payments in more than 135 currencies to over 180 countries and receive funds in 13 currencies through their Citi Vietnam accounts.
Innovations such as tokenized deposits and programmable payments could further improve cross-border liquidity management. However, technological advances must be accompanied by strong regulation and sound governance.
Citi has operated in Vietnam for more than three decades. What does its long-term commitment to the market look like today?
Citi opened a representative office in Hanoi in 1993 and became the first U.S. financial institution licensed to open a branch in Vietnam in 1994.
We have since refined our global strategy around four businesses: Services, Markets, Banking and Wealth. In Vietnam, we focus on institutional clients through these capabilities.
We are growing across nearly every geography, including Vietnam, and aim to support clients wherever they operate. Our businesses in more than 90 markets are largely staffed and led by local professionals. Our Vietnam franchise, under Minh Ngo's leadership, reflects this approach.
Citi has supported several of Vietnam's development priorities. We recently helped finance the completion of PV Power's Nhon Trach 3 and 4 power plants, which are set to become Vietnam's first liquefied natural gas-to-power facilities.
We have also provided more than $100 million in social trade advance facilities to the Joint Stock Commercial Bank for Investment and Development of Vietnam (BIDV) and Military Commercial Joint Stock Bank (MB), supporting lending to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.
In September, Citi and Ho Chi Minh City Development Joint Stock Commercial Bank (HDBank) signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation across banking and financial services. We see the agreement as a basis for deeper collaboration and support for businesses and the wider economy.
Looking ahead, we see opportunities in infrastructure, energy, advanced manufacturing, semiconductors, AI, digital infrastructure and capital markets. As Vietnam moves up the value chain, we look forward to helping our clients achieve their ambitions.
